text: The on-prem server never had real monitoring -- if it slowed down, nobody found out until a customer complained. This lesson adds exactly that: basic monitoring and one real alert, the thing the old server never had.

The moment vm-catalog01 existed, Azure Monitor already started collecting platform metrics for it -- CPU, network, disk -- with zero setup, retained 93 days by default. That's already more visibility than the on-prem server ever had.

Before building an alert, Theo checks what normal looks like in Metrics Explorer, switching the aggregation from Average to Maximum -- the same CPU data can look fine on average while spiking to dangerous levels the average hides.

Logs need somewhere to live before they can be queried, so Theo creates a Log Analytics workspace -- law-driftwood-catalog -- and points the VM's diagnostic settings at it. Once logs flow, a KQL query against the Activity Log can answer who changed what, and when.

One real alert: average CPU over 80% for 5 minutes, checked every minute. That evaluation window matters as much as the threshold -- without it, a two-second spike that's completely normal would trigger a noisy, useless alert.

The alert's action points at a reusable Action Group -- ag-driftwood-ops -- emailing both Theo and Priya, so the same notification setup can attach to this alert and to future alerts without rebuilding it each time. Next lesson tests the whole migrated app end to end, images, VM, and monitoring together, before cutover.
